title: The Historical Actor Murder Case
notes: Recurring detective-cast nodes (Conan, Kogoro Mouri, Ran, Inspector Megure, Officer Takagi) omitted by convention -- their actions surface indirectly through object/location edges (e.g. the model gun's fingerprint evidence, the elevator inspection) rather than as person nodes. No `event` node type: every action is a directly typed, attributed edge between the entities involved, sharing an `order` integer so edges belonging to the same real-world occurrence can be grouped. No (Flashback)-tagged lines occur anywhere in either transcript -- the whole case (including the bankruptcy/affair backstory) is delivered as present-tense dialogue/confession, so every edge is temporal_frame: present except the standing structural facts (relationship, has_motive_against, owns, implicates) which carry no order/temporal_frame at all, per schema. Small named cast (only 3 named non-recurring characters appear across both episodes) -- this is a two-person-apartment locked-scene mystery, not a large-ensemble case, so the node count is genuinely smaller than ep011's. case_type: murder.

clues.desc: The living rooms on the 5th and 6th floors are furnished and arranged identically -- same TV, sofa, curtains, and table position -- with the only difference being four used teacups on the 5th-floor table versus a bare 6th-floor table. Comparing the two rooms is what proves the 6th floor was a deliberate duplicate built to disguise which floor the Mouri party had actually been on.

The phone sound heard on the balcony when Isami's body fell does not match the ringtone of the phone Officer Takagi calls at the end (Kogoro's own phone, coincidentally the same model Hijikata tried to mimic) -- comparing the two rings exposes that the balcony sound came from Hijikata's decoy phone, not Okita's genuine one, since Okita had switched phones the day before.

When the group first saw Isami collapse, only her upper body was visible outside the window with her legs still in the room; by the time the door was forced open, her whole body was out on the balcony. Comparing these two observed body positions initially reads as proof someone (presumably Okita) dragged the body in a panic -- but is later re-explained by the delayed, timed release of the fishing-line rig completing her fall on its own.
